title: Travel & places
text:
Niagara Falls
FIELD NOTES / A DIFFERENT PACE
Some places make it easier to slow down and pay attention. Here, the movement of the water and the scale of the landscape are a reminder to look beyond the frame of a photograph.
I’m interested in the small details that make a place feel different: how people move through it, where they gather, and what they stop to notice.

title: Travel & places
text:
What I want to remember

The details that a photograph doesn’t capture.
A question about the place or the people who live there.
Something I would notice differently on a return visit.

title: What a chart can tell me
text: A chart makes some patterns easier to see, but it also reflects a series of choices. Which observations belong in the plot? What belongs on each axis? Which differences deserve attention?

title: What a chart can tell me
text:
One choice that matters
In a comparison of income and life expectancy, a logarithmic income axis changes the spacing of the values. That can help reveal patterns that are difficult to see when a few large values stretch the scale.

title: What a chart can tell me
section: What I still need to ask
text:
What I still need to ask
A visible association does not explain why the pattern exists. Before moving from description to explanation, I need to think about the research question, the data, and possible alternative explanations.
My next step is to describe the plot in one careful sentence, then write down a question it cannot answer.

title: Your website: start here
text:
A small Quarto website for students. Five tabs, ordinary text files, and one folder for all your photos. No extra extensions, Python setup, or publication spreadsheets are needed.
First goal: replace the name, introduction, email, and two sample photos. Preview the result before changing anything else. All page text and experiences are examples to replace with your own.


A fork is your copy of this repository on GitHub. A clone is the copy on your computer that you edit in RStudio.

Sign in to GitHub and open the course template.
Click Fork, select your own account as the owner, and click Create fork. You can keep the repository name.
On your fork, click Code > HTTPS and copy the repository URL. Check that the repository owner in the URL is your own GitHub username.
In RStudio, choose File > New Project > Version Control > Git. Paste your fork’s URL, choose where to save the project, and click Create Project.
Continue with the preview steps below. Your future Commit and Push actions will update your own fork.

If Version Control > Git is unavailable, complete the course’s Git setup first. If you already cloned your fork, just open the included .Rproj file.




Open quarto-academic-website-template.Rproj in RStudio. Keep the whole folder together.
Open index.qmd. Use Source mode to see the short comments explaining what to edit.
Click Render to preview the home page. For a complete site preview, use the Build pane’s Render Website button (called Render in some versions).
Edit, save, and render again. The generated pages go into docs/.

Use a recent RStudio with Quarto support. If Render is missing, reopen the .Rproj and check that Quarto is available in RStudio. This starter contains no executable R code, so it needs no R packages.

├── README.md                 Start here

The hidden .git folder holds version history if you cloned this repository. RStudio may also create local folders such as .Rproj.user and .quarto. You do not need to edit them.
Your writing lives in .qmd files. _design/ holds the appearance; docs/ holds what Quarto builds. Editing a file in docs/ will not update the source and may be overwritten on the next render.




In _quarto.yml, replace Your Name and the site description. Leave the project and metadata-files sections as they are.
In index.qmd, replace the name, short subtitle, introduction, and you@example.com.
Replace the home photo as described below.
Update the short sections beneath the introduction, then render.
Edit the other pages and replace every sample experience before sharing the site.

Most edits are ordinary text. Keep the opening and closing --- lines at the top of each page; the lines between them set its title and other options. Keep indentation in _quarto.yml. On the home page, keep the ::: layout lines in place while changing the words between them. Text between <!-- and --> is a helpful comment and does not appear on the website.



The two included photos came from the original template:

images/profile.jpg: home page (currently flowers).
images/travel.jpg: travel page (currently Niagara Falls).

The easiest replacement is your own image with the same filename and extension. If you prefer a different filename, update the page’s image path. JPG and PNG are good starting choices. Names such as campus-walk.jpg are easier to use than names with spaces. Export a phone’s HEIC photo as JPG or PNG first.
In a main page:
![](images/campus-walk.jpg){fig-alt="Students walking across campus"}
Inside a post in posts/:
![](../images/campus-walk.jpg){fig-alt="Students walking across campus"}
The fig-alt text describes the image for someone who cannot see it. Replace that description as well as the filename. To show a caption below the photo, put the caption between the empty [] brackets. More examples are in images/README.md.
For this local workflow, you copy images into images/; there is no separate website upload form. When you later commit and push the source and rendered site, the images go with them.




Open **_design/new-post.qmd** in RStudio.
Choose File > Save As. Save it inside posts/ with a new name, such as my-first-post.qmd. Keep the .qmd extension.
Change the title, date (YYYY-MM-DD), and one-sentence description at the top.
Replace the sample paragraphs with your writing. Add a photo if useful.
Save and render the whole website from the Build pane. The Blog list updates automatically, newest first. You do not need to add a link manually.

To remove a sample post, delete that .qmd file from posts/ and render the website again. To keep a work-in-progress post private, keep its file outside this repository until ready to share; hiding a link is not the same as keeping its source private.

You can also use RStudio’s Visual editor for ordinary writing. Source mode is useful when following the comments or changing image filenames.
To add a resume later, create a files/ folder, put resume.pdf there, and add [My resume](files/resume.pdf) to career.qmd. You do not need a resume file to use this template.



Preview locally first. When your content is ready and your repository is connected to GitHub:

In RStudio, render the whole website. Confirm the generated docs/ pages look right.
In the Git pane, inspect your source changes and the updated docs/ files, stage them, Commit, then Push. Include new images and the supplied .nojekyll file. This publishing workflow intentionally tracks docs/.
On your own GitHub repository, open Settings > Pages. Under Build and deployment, choose Deploy from a branch, select main and /docs, then Save.
Open the website address GitHub provides after deployment finishes.
Optionally, uncomment site-url in _quarto.yml and paste that exact address. Render, commit, and push again.

Future updates use the same edit, render, commit, push sequence. Commit and Push alone do not render your changes. A normal repository produces a URL ending in its repository name; a repository named exactly YOUR-USERNAME.github.io uses that account’s root website address. Follow any repository visibility or account-plan requirements shown by GitHub Pages.
If you rename or delete a published page or post, remove its old generated .html from docs/ (or delete docs/ and render the whole website to rebuild it) before pushing. This avoids leaving an old page accessible at its previous address.

title: Academic interests & research
text:
I’m interested in how people participate in public life, how communities differ, and how data can help us ask better questions about both.

Political participation: Who gets involved, and what makes participation easier?
Cities and communities: How do local environments shape everyday choices?
Data and communication: How can a chart make a complex pattern easier to understand?

title: Academic interests & research
text:
A project I’m developing

Comparing life expectancy across countries
COURSE PROJECT · IN PROGRESS
Question. How does life expectancy vary with income across countries in a given year?
Approach. Use R to explore the historical Gapminder data and make a clearly labeled visualization.
What I’m learning. Choosing the year, scale, and unit of analysis changes what readers can see. An association in a plot is a starting point for questions, not evidence of a causal effect.
Read a reflection on this project

title: Academic interests & research
text:
What comes next
I’d like to compare the same countries over time and consider what these measures leave out.
